studies.title: Broomsedge Bluestem
studies.tagline: An abundant native grass with promising potential as a botanical colorant
studies.statusNote: The wool dye readings come from the original study. The lake pigment method below is a proposal and has not been run yet.
studies.alt: A dense stand of copper-orange broomsedge bluestem grass under a blue sky

body: This case study investigates Broomsedge Bluestem (Andropogon virginicus), a native warm-season perennial grass that grows abundantly across my property in Tennessee. Its accessibility, adaptability, and initial dye performance made it one of the first botanical materials selected for experimentation in my investigation of locally available natural colorants.

Preliminary dyeing experiments produced noticeable yellow-to-brown coloration, accompanied by encouraging results in color strength and fastness. These observations suggest that Broomsedge may contain recoverable color-bearing compounds with potential applications beyond conventional textile dyeing.

The purpose of this investigation is to characterize its dyeing properties, examine the chemical behavior of its extracted colorants, and explore methods of converting its aqueous extract into a concentrated, dry, shelf-stable pigment.

Rather than treating Broomsedge as simply another natural dye source, this study considers its potential as a locally abundant raw material for producing a standardized botanical colorant suitable for textile applications, pigment formulation, and further chemical investigation.

Despite its common name, Broomsedge Bluestem is a true grass belonging to the family Poaceae, rather than a member of the sedge family Cyperaceae. It is a relatively slender, bunch-forming perennial characterized by upright stems and narrow leaves, and it grows in distinct clumps rather than the dense, spreading growth of many other grasses.

One of its most recognizable characteristics is its seasonal color transformation. During active growth, its foliage is predominantly green to yellow-green. As the growing season progresses, the stems and leaves develop copper, bronze, and orange-brown coloration before eventually fading into straw-colored tones.

Its flowering structures are relatively inconspicuous. The inflorescences consist of slender racemes bearing small spikelets with characteristic silky hairs, partially enclosed by modified leaves called spathes.

The seasonal accumulation of standing dead foliage is particularly relevant to this investigation. It provides an opportunity to compare material harvested at different developmental stages and determine whether maturity influences the concentration or composition of extractable colorants.

Broomsedge Bluestem is native to Tennessee and much of the eastern United States. It is particularly common in open, sunny environments, including old fields, pastures, roadsides, woodland openings, and other disturbed habitats.

The species is notably adaptable to poor growing conditions. It frequently establishes itself in nutrient-depleted, eroded, and low-fertility soils, where other vegetation may struggle to compete. Although it is particularly associated with sandy soils, it can tolerate a broader range of soil conditions.

Its abundance on my property makes it an especially practical candidate for repeated experimentation. Rather than relying on scarce, cultivated, or commercially sourced botanical materials, I can investigate a readily available native species and collect material across multiple growing seasons.

This accessibility also provides an opportunity to investigate seasonal and environmental variation. Differences in soil conditions, plant maturity, growing conditions, and harvesting time may influence the chemical composition of the extracted colorants.

Initial experiments with Broomsedge Bluestem produced yellow-to-brown coloration when applied to textile material. The preliminary results were encouraging, particularly regarding color strength and resistance to deterioration during initial fastness observations.

body.note: These results justify further investigation, but they should not yet be interpreted as evidence of a standardized or chemically characterized dye.

body: Plant-derived colorants can originate from several classes of naturally occurring compounds, including flavonoids, tannins, and other phenolic substances. However, the specific compounds responsible for Broomsedge's extracted coloration have not yet been identified through chemical analysis, so it would be premature to attribute its dyeing performance to any particular pigment family.

ul: Differences in coloration between leaves, stems, and flowering structures.
The influence of harvesting season and plant maturity.
The effects of extraction temperature and duration.
Differences between unmordanted and mordanted textile samples.
Resistance to light, washing, and water exposure.
The chemical behavior of extracted colorants during precipitation and recovery.

body: These experiments will help establish whether Broomsedge is a viable and reproducible source of botanical color.
Broomsedge Bluestem is particularly interesting because of the combination of its local abundance, adaptability to low-fertility environments, and promising preliminary dye results.

Traditional natural dye research often focuses on well-established sources such as madder, weld, indigo, and various tree barks. This investigation instead considers whether a common native grass, not traditionally recognized as a major commercial dye source, can provide a useful alternative.

Its abundance also makes it suitable for repeated sampling and comparative experimentation. Multiple harvests can be evaluated using standardized extraction and testing procedures, allowing differences between batches to be measured rather than treated as unavoidable variation.
Ultimately, the objective is to determine whether Broomsedge can be developed into a reproducible botanical colorant with practical applications beyond its original use as a textile dye.

sections.h: 6. Proposed methodology: a dry, shelf-stable lake pigment
body: One potential direction for developing Broomsedge Bluestem as a botanical colorant is converting its aqueous dye extract into a concentrated, dry, shelf-stable pigment. Liquid extracts can be inconvenient to store, transport, measure, and distribute, and their concentration can change through evaporation, microbial growth, and prolonged storage. A recovered solid pigment would offer a more manageable alternative.

The proposed method extracts water-soluble color-bearing compounds from Broomsedge and then attempts to recover them through aluminum-based precipitation. The intended product is an aluminum-containing botanical lake pigment: an insoluble or poorly water-soluble solid in which organic colorants are associated with an inorganic aluminum-containing phase.

This approach is based on established aluminum lake-pigment preparation techniques. Aluminum salts, including potassium alum, have been used to recover natural colorants from aqueous plant extracts through controlled precipitation around pH 5.0–5.5.

body.note: The effectiveness of this method for Broomsedge has not yet been established. Open each stage below for the details.

ul: Dried Broomsedge Bluestem (Andropogon virginicus).
Distilled or deionized water (H₂O).
Potassium aluminum sulfate dodecahydrate, commonly known as potassium alum or potash alum.
Chemical formula: KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O.
Potassium Aluminum Sulfate (KAl(SO₄)₂), prepared as a dilute aqueous solution.
Soda Ash (Na₂CO₃), prepared as a dilute aqueous solution.
Balance.
Thermometer.
5 Gallon stainless steel vat (inert with the chemicals used).
Plastic pitchers with measurement markings(inert with the chemicals used).
Cotton filter.
Drying dishes.
Airtight storage containers.

body: The potassium alum provides the aluminum ions necessary for the proposed lake-pigment formation. Soda ash and additional potassium alum provide controlled upward and downward pH adjustment. The use of dilute solutions makes incremental pH adjustments easier to control, and the actual amount required will depend on the acidity and buffering capacity of each extract.

sections.h: 6.2 Stage one: botanical preparation and extraction
body: Plant material should be collected from identified Broomsedge populations and separated according to the plant parts being investigated. Leaves, stems, and flowering structures may be extracted independently in later experiments. The material should be dried to a consistent condition before weighing, and the dry mass recorded, because moisture differences would otherwise introduce variation.

ol: Add the material to 20 mL of distilled or deionized water for every gram.
Heat the mixture at a controlled temperature, initially testing approximately 80 °C.
Maintain the extraction for 60 minutes with occasional stirring.
Filter the extract to remove plant fibers and suspended botanical material.
Record the recovered liquid volume, temperature, appearance, and pH.
Weigh remaining leaf litter seperately, then repeat the process a second time.

body: These conditions are an initial experimental baseline rather than an established optimum. Additional experiments should investigate how extraction temperature, duration, and plant-to-water ratio affect color recovery. The resulting liquid is the crude aqueous Broomsedge extract, and its initial pH and color should be recorded before proceeding.

sections.h: 6.3 Stage two: preparation of the aluminum solution
body: Potassium aluminum sulfate dodecahydrate, KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O, will serve as the aluminum source. When dissolved in water, potassium alum dissociates and provides hydrated aluminum ions, which can interact with certain plant-derived organic compounds. The relevant aluminum species can undergo hydrolysis and form aluminum hydroxide under appropriate conditions. A simplified representation of the precipitation reaction is:
The formation of aluminum hydroxide provides an insoluble inorganic phase that may capture or incorporate organic colorants.

body.note: It is important to distinguish this reaction from the formation of an actual lake pigment. Producing aluminum hydroxide alone does not demonstrate that the Broomsedge colorants have been incorporated into the solid.

body: For the initial experiments, a potassium alum solution should be prepared separately using distilled water. Its concentration and the total quantity added to each extract should be recorded. The amount of alum will be treated as an experimental variable rather than assumed to have a universally optimal concentration.

sections.h: 6.4 Stage three: controlled precipitation through pH titration
body: This stage is the central chemical component of the proposed methodology. The objective is to encourage the formation of an insoluble aluminum-containing material capable of carrying the extracted Broomsedge colorants.

First, a measured volume of filtered extract is placed into a clean glass beaker. The predetermined quantity of dissolved potassium alum is then introduced under continuous stirring. After the alum has been incorporated, the pH is adjusted gradually using the dilute soda ash solution. The solution should be monitored continuously with a calibrated pH meter, with reagent additions made incrementally and the mixture allowed to equilibrate between additions.

The range is intended to identify conditions under which color-bearing material can be recovered efficiently. Published research on aluminum-based natural dye lakes has demonstrated precipitation around pH 5.0–5.5, which is a useful starting point, although Broomsedge may behave differently depending on the compounds in its extract.

Precipitate formation should be monitored through changes in turbidity, visible flocculation, sediment formation, and changes in the coloration of the remaining liquid. Following pH adjustment, the suspension should equilibrate under consistent conditions before separation. The amount of soda ash required to reach each target pH should be recorded, which will help establish the acid-base behavior of the extract and improve reproducibility between batches.

body.note: Chemical consideration: aluminum hydroxide is amphoteric. It can dissolve under sufficiently acidic or alkaline conditions, so excessive soda ash may not improve recovery and can instead promote soluble aluminate species. The pH must be controlled rather than simply increased until a precipitate appears.

body: Once precipitation has occurred, the suspension will contain the recovered solid and a remaining liquid phase. The precipitate will be separated by filtration and then washed with measured quantities of distilled or deionized water. Washing serves several purposes:

ul: Removing residual potassium and sulfate salts.
Removing excess soluble aluminum-containing species.
Removing unreacted pH-adjustment reagents.
Reducing soluble botanical impurities.

body: The wash water should be collected and observed rather than immediately discarded. A strongly colored filtrate or wash solution may indicate that desired color-bearing compounds remain dissolved or are being lost during purification. The color of the original extract, the post-precipitation supernatant, and the wash water should all be documented.

A successful recovery should ideally produce a visibly colored solid while leaving a comparatively depleted supernatant. Visual observations alone cannot establish the chemical composition of the recovered material.

sections.h: 6.6 Stage five: drying and powder preparation
body: The recovered solid will be transferred to a clean drying dish and dried under controlled, low-temperature conditions to minimize possible thermal degradation or oxidation of the organic colorants. An initial drying temperature of approximately 40–50 °C can be investigated, with the final condition selected according to the stability of the recovered material.

The solid should be dried until repeated mass measurements show a reasonably stable mass. It can then be gently broken apart and ground into a uniform powder, and stored in an airtight, moisture-resistant container protected from unnecessary exposure to light, heat, and humidity.
The objective is a concentrated, reproducible botanical pigment that can be weighed, stored, transported, and used in subsequent experiments.

Success should not be judged solely by the appearance or total mass of the recovered powder. Several measurements are needed to determine whether the process yields a useful and reproducible colorant.
The recovered dry mass is compared with the original mass of dried Broomsedge.

body.formula: Recovery yield (%) = (m dry product ÷ m dry plant) × 100

body: The recovered mass includes both organic and inorganic material, so it should not be interpreted as the mass of pure dye.

The original extract and the recovered pigment should be characterized with consistent color-measurement procedures, which may include CIELAB coordinates (L*, a*, b*) and CIE76 color differences (the same ΔE used elsewhere in this archive; see the Methods tab). This allows the color of the original extract to be compared with the reconstituted pigment and later textile applications. HEX values may also be recorded as convenient digital approximations of measured color.

The remaining supernatant should be compared with the original extract to estimate how much coloration remains in solution. Where appropriate, UV-visible spectrophotometry can give a more quantitative comparison of absorbance before and after precipitation.

Standardized wool samples should be dyed using the original liquid extract and the recovered pigment preparation, then compared for color strength, CIELAB coordinates, and overall appearance. A separate test should investigate whether the recovered pigment can be dispersed effectively in a textile dyebath.

ul: Light exposure.
Washing.
Water exposure.

body: These tests will establish whether precipitation and drying preserve the practical dyeing performance seen in the original liquid extract.

The powder should be evaluated periodically for changes in color, moisture uptake, physical condition, and reconstitution behavior, to determine whether it meaningfully improves shelf stability over the liquid extract.
To distinguish genuine pigment recovery from ordinary aluminum hydroxide precipitation, several controls are necessary.

head: Group
What it is
What it tells us
rows: Extract goes through the same pH adjustment with no potassium alum.
Whether the color-bearing compounds precipitate on their own from pH changes alone.
Potassium alum solution goes through the same pH adjustment in distilled water.
The appearance and recovery of the inorganic precipitate without botanical colorants.
An untreated portion of the original extract is retained.
A baseline for color, absorbance, and chemical behavior.
Extract with alum and controlled pH adjustment.
Whether colorants are incorporated into the aluminum-containing precipitate.

body: Comparing the recovered solids and remaining liquids across these groups will provide stronger evidence of whether the plant-derived colorants are being incorporated into the precipitate.

Each condition should ideally be repeated at least three times. Plant mass, water volume, extraction temperature, extraction duration, alum concentration, final pH, and drying conditions should be held constant whenever they are not the variable under investigation.

The intended product is a dry, aluminum-based Broomsedge lake pigment containing recovered organic colorants associated with an inorganic aluminum-containing phase. Its precise composition cannot currently be predicted because the identity and concentration of Broomsedge's extracted colorants have not been established.

The recovered material may contain aluminum hydroxide, aluminum-associated organic compounds, residual inorganic salts, and other co-precipitated botanical substances. It is therefore important to avoid assuming that every colored precipitate is a chemically defined lake pigment.

A lake pigment is also not equivalent to a conventional water-soluble dye powder. Precipitation may reduce the solubility of the original color-bearing compounds, so the material may disperse as fine particles rather than dissolve. A pigment suitable for paints, inks, and other particulate color formulations may not perform well in a conventional textile dyebath, and a material that keeps useful textile dyeing characteristics may not have the properties of a stable artists' pigment. These applications must be evaluated independently.

A liquid Broomsedge extract has limited practicality: it needs suitable storage, takes up more space in transport, and may degrade or support microbial growth. A concentrated, dry pigment could be weighed and distributed in standardized quantities, incorporated into different formulations, and stored without keeping a large volume of aqueous extract.

Its potential applications extend beyond textile dyeing. Artists, paint formulators, printmakers, educational institutions, and researchers may all have an interest in locally sourced botanical pigments, a broader market than natural textile dyers alone. Actual commercial suitability would depend on pigment performance, batch consistency, shelf stability, safety evaluation, and production costs.

Plants are biological organisms, and their chemical composition is not identical between individual specimens, harvests, or growing seasons, so equal masses of different Broomsedge harvests may not yield equivalent amounts of extractable colorant. A standardized extraction and precipitation procedure would make these differences measurable. Future work could characterize the recovered pigment by dry mass, aluminum content, phenolic content, and spectroscopic properties, allowing batches to be compared more meaningfully.
Once recovered, the pigment could serve as a standardized starting material for additional investigations:

ul: Combining Broomsedge pigment with other botanical lake pigments.
Investigating different aluminum-to-colorant ratios.
Comparing alternative extraction and precipitation conditions.
Studying the influence of pH on pigment formation.
Evaluating pigment compatibility with different binders.
Investigating the relationship between organic colorant concentration and observed color strength.
Comparing the chemical and physical properties of pigments from different harvests.

body.note: The proposed precipitation process remains theoretical for Broomsedge Bluestem.

body: Although aluminum-based lake-pigment production is an established method for certain botanical extracts, the chemical composition of Broomsedge's extracted colorants has not yet been established. It is unknown whether its color-bearing compounds will precipitate efficiently, form stable associations with aluminum-containing solids, or keep their original coloration after drying and storage.

The initial investigation will focus on whether precipitation is feasible and which conditions maximize useful color recovery. Later work should investigate the composition of the recovered pigment and whether its physical and chemical characteristics suit textile, artistic, or other applications. UV-visible spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and elemental analysis could provide further information about the recovered material.

Ultimately, the objective is a reproducible method for converting an abundant native grass into a concentrated botanical colorant. If successful, this would provide a foundation for further research into the chemical properties, practical applications, and commercial potential of Broomsedge Bluestem as a source of natural pigment.
